summary: Defines the Binary extension to IMAP4, which lets a client and server exchange message body data without a MIME content-transfer encoding such as Base64. The server does any decoding and the client gets the raw data. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Email attachments are usually wrapped in a special code to travel safely, then unwrapped. This memo lets a mail program ask the server to do the unwrapping, so the file arrives ready to use.

subtitle: Lets an IMAP server decode attachments itself, so the client gets raw bytes instead of Base64 text.

tldr.problem: Message bodies are usually MIME-encoded (for example with base64) to survive transports that cannot carry binary data, and that encoding adds overhead on slow links.
tldr.mechanism: The Binary extension adds FETCH BINARY, BINARY.PEEK and BINARY.SIZE, so the server removes the content-transfer-encoding before sending, and adds a new eight-bit transparent literal called literal8.
tldr.outcome: Clients get decoded data and save resources, but they SHOULD still be able to do their own decoding. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 4466.

today: RFC 3516 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 4466. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Skip the Encoding
sections.content:
MIME lets email carry non-text content. Because traditional mail transports cannot always pass binary data transparently, MIME defines content-transfer-encodings (CTE), such as base64, that make the content safe to send.

That encoding has a cost. The RFC says the overhead can be considerable in some settings, for example slow radio links and streaming multimedia. The Binary extension to IMAP4 lets the server perform the CTE decoding before it sends message data to the client.
sections.eli5: Wrapping a gift in lots of paper makes the parcel bigger. This extension lets the post office unwrap it first, so less has to be carried to you.

sections.title: Decoding and the Domain of the Data
sections.content:
Every IMAP4 body section has a CTE. A section with no explicit Content-Transfer-Encoding header is implicitly labeled 7bit. The CTE specifies both a decoding algorithm and the domain of the decoded data.

Some CTEs are identity encodings, so no decoding is needed. Their data may still not be expressible in base IMAP4, for example MIME binary content that contains NUL octets. For these cases the extension introduces a new kind of literal that is fully eight bit transparent.

So the server does two logical steps for a FETCH BINARY: it performs any CTE-related decoding, then it determines the domain of the decoded data. The second step decides which protocol element carries the data.
sections.eli5: First the server unwraps the parcel. Then it checks what kind of thing is inside, so it knows which box to put it in for the trip to you.

sections.title: The FETCH and CAPABILITY Extensions
sections.content:
A server that supports the extension MUST include BINARY in its CAPABILITY response. The extension adds three FETCH data items:

  • BINARY[section]<partial> asks for the section after CTE decoding. A partial request works like a partial FETCH BODY, except that the offsets refer to the decoded data.
  • BINARY.PEEK is the same but does not implicitly set the \Seen flag.
  • BINARY.SIZE asks for the decoded size of the section, which is the size to expect from the matching FETCH BINARY.

The response carries the content as an nstring or a literal8. If the decoded data is 8bit and has no NUL octet, the server SHOULD use a normal string rather than a literal8, so the client can tell there are no NULs without scanning. The size returned by BINARY.SIZE MUST match the size of the data in the corresponding FETCH BINARY.

If the server cannot decode the section's CTE, it MUST fail the request with a NO response carrying the UNKNOWN-CTE response code.

BINARY.SIZE may be expensive for some servers, because they may have to calculate the value every time. Clients should not request it needlessly.
sections.eli5: You can ask for the unwrapped file, for just a peek at it, or for how big it will be. If the post office does not know how to unwrap it, it says no and tells you why.

sections.title: Appending Binary Data
sections.content:
The APPEND command is extended so a client can store data that contains NULs, by using the literal8 syntax. The server MAY change the CTE of the appended data, but the change MUST NOT lose any data.

If the destination mailbox cannot store binary content, the server MUST fail the request with a NO response carrying UNKNOWN-CTE.
sections.eli5: The same trick works in the other direction. You can hand over a raw file to store, and the server must never damage it.

sections.title: Headers, Line Endings and Client Duties
sections.content:
MIME encoded header text (the non-ASCII encoding from RFC 2047) is a different mechanism from the body CTE. A server MUST NOT convert it in response to any binary FETCH or APPEND.

Servers MUST send textual line-oriented sections with IMAP4 CRLF line endings, whatever the stored form. A server may store binary content unencoded, but it MUST still issue BODYSTRUCTURE responses as though binary sections were in a CTE the base specification accepts, and FETCH BODY MUST return content in the format BODYSTRUCTURE describes.

The RFC warns that changing the CTE of appended literal8 data should be done only when absolutely necessary, because gratuitous changes make most cryptographic operations on the message useless. It also says this is an optimization, not a replacement for basic client functionality, so clients that support it SHOULD be prepared to do their own CTE decoding.
sections.eli5: The server must keep the labels on the parcel honest and not tamper with signed letters. Your mail program should still know how to unwrap things itself, just in case.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The grammar is given in ABNF and augments the IMAP4rev1 grammar from RFC 3501. It extends append, fetch-att, msg-att-static and resp-text-code, and defines literal8, partial and section-binary.

A literal8 begins with a tilde, then a brace-enclosed octet count, then CRLF, then that many octets of any value.
sections.eli5: This part is the exact spelling rules, so every mail program writes the new commands the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that there are no known additional security issues beyond those in the base IMAP4rev1 protocol. Its separate warning about gratuitous encoding changes breaking cryptographic operations on messages is covered above.
sections.eli5: This extension does not add any new danger beyond what ordinary IMAP already has.

data.title: Binary extension grammar
data.code:
fetch-att      =/  "BINARY" [".PEEK"] section-binary [partial]
                   / "BINARY.SIZE" section-binary

literal8       =   "~{" number "}" CRLF *OCTET

msg-att-static =/  "BINARY" section-binary SP (nstring / literal8)
                   / "BINARY.SIZE" section-binary SP number

partial        =   "<" number "." nz-number ">"

resp-text-code =/  "UNKNOWN-CTE"

section-binary =   "[" [section-part] "]"
